anchors.label: The new king does not know Joseph and describes Israel as more numerous and mightier than his own people.
Shiphrah and Puah receive the king’s command, fear God, and keep the boys alive.
Each household takes a lamb, with neighboring households sharing when one is too small.
The firstborn deaths are described from Pharaoh’s throne to the captive in the dungeon and include livestock.
The passage names men on foot, children, a mixed multitude, flocks, herds, and livestock moving from Rameses to Succoth.
Pharaoh is expected to describe Israel as entangled and shut in; later he and his servants regret releasing them.
Moses and Israel sing first; Miriam later leads the women with tambourines and dances.
The song gives the enemy a first-person plan to pursue, overtake, divide plunder, and destroy.
God sends Moses to Pharaoh; Moses asks who he is to go, and the answer begins with promised presence.
Zipporah uses a flint, circumcises her son, casts the foreskin at his feet, and speaks of a bridegroom of blood.
Israelite officers appeal to Pharaoh after being beaten for missing a quota they cannot reduce.
Some servants fear the LORD’s word and bring people and livestock inside; others leave them in the field.
